A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SemInfo constituency-parsing research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on five PCFG variants across four languages, correlation analyses, and constituent-type recall results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds optimization comparisons, paraphraser robustness experiments, and parser-agreement analyses.

M1.justification: v1 specifies TreeCRF REINFORCE with an average reward baseline. v2 retains this as Posterior-Avg but introduces V-function baselines, stepwise optimization with generalized advantage estimation, and direct PCFG-based counterparts in Appendix A.1. These are substantive alternative training procedures.

E1.justification: Coverage remains constituency parsing on English PTB, Chinese CTB 5.1, and French/German SPMRL. The added studies vary optimization, supervision, and paraphraser configurations; they introduce no additional corpus, language, domain, or parsing task.

E2.justification: v2 adds supervised TreeCRF/PCFG reference models in Table 5, a right-branching baseline in Table 6, and heterogeneous agreement comparisons including ContextDistort and DIORA in Figure 13. Conversely, Table 3 removes StructFormer, reported at 54 English sentence-F1 in v1. These substantially expand and revise the comparison set.

E3.justification: The original splits, model sizes, preprocessing, and parsing metrics remain unchanged. New protocols compare training distributions and optimization strategies with supervised controls, vary seven paraphrasing models in Table 6, and evaluate pairwise parser agreement in Appendix A.6. The SF1i/SF1c terminology clarifies existing metrics rather than changing them.

E4.justification: New Appendices A.1, A.5, and A.6 investigate optimization choices, sensitivity to paraphraser quality, and diversity relevant to ensembling. Figure 8 expands sentence-level correlation examples, and Section 5.2 adds vocabulary-shift statistics. The earlier training-stage correlation and constituent-recall analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The original three-run mean/standard-deviation reporting, two-tailed t-tests, eight independently seeded correlation models, and Fisher Z aggregation remain unchanged. Additional tables extend the existing uncertainty-reporting format without specifying a new statistical procedure or increased run count.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark, correlation, and constituent-recall values are unchanged, apart from the removed StructFormer result. New Tables 5–6 and agreement figures add substantial results: Table 6 reports SemInfo-NPCFG scores from 59.01 with Qwen2.5-0.5B to 66.85 with GPT-3.5. Table 5 explicitly reports retrained comparisons, not replacements for Table 1.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds formal sampling distributions, value and advantage functions, dynamic-programming recurrences, and alternative optimization objectives. The stated TreeCRF distribution also changes from a sum of span posteriors in v1 Equation 4 to a product in v2 Equation 11. The original span-posterior proof survives as Appendix A.2.

C1.justification: v1 claims new state-of-the-art results in three languages. v2 qualifies the contribution as state-of-the-art-level performance from a non-ensemble model. The central SemInfo objective, correlation claim, and reported average 7.85-point improvement remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning robustness to noisy paraphrases, similar accuracy across optimization strategies, TreeCRF computational advantages, and possible PCFG expressivity limits suggested by supervised comparisons. Appendix A.6 introduces an agreement-based argument for potential ensemble benefits, without reporting an actual ensemble improvement. Section 3 also explicitly states the paraphraser-quality assumption.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project code-availability link, sampling and V-function computation details, and attribution of reused parser predictions to Shayegh et al. It also reports relative training speed and memory use. Existing dataset-processing instructions and paraphrasing prompts are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to mean-field reinforcement learning, generalized advantage estimation, recurrent neural network grammars, and ensemble distillation, while removing the StructFormer reference. It qualifies positioning around non-ensemble parsing; the main related-work discussion and relationship to Chen et al. remain substantially intact.

P1.justification: v2 clarifies instance-level versus corpus-level F1 terminology, expands the training explanation, simplifies the substring-frequency exposition, and adjusts abstract and conclusion wording. Existing sections largely retain their organization and prose; much of the appendix growth is new scientific content rather than wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds a training-pipeline diagram, optimization tables, two algorithm displays, a paraphraser comparison table, expanded correlation examples, and agreement heatmaps. Existing figures are repositioned and relabeled, and training-curve F1 axes change to percentage units. The enlarged training-curve display also overlaps the page-number area.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses two important gaps in v1: dependence on one paraphraser and limited evidence for the chosen optimization strategy. Tables 5–6 provide direct alternative-strategy and paraphraser-quality comparisons, while procedural detail, code-access information, and narrower performance claims improve assessability. Some weaknesses remain: ensemble benefits are only inferred, and the claimed 9-point robustness gain is 8.05 points in Table 6. These limited issues do not outweigh the stronger validation of central design choices.
